title: Mazel Tov, Dummies!

jokes.text: If it's positive, 'Awesome! We're having a baby! I wanna name it Frisbee!' If it's negative, 'Awesome. We're not gonna fight about the name Frisbee, and we get disco fries for breakfast 'cause we're sad.'
jokes.setup: Criss and Liz are looking at a pregnancy test. Criss says 'This is a win-win.'
jokes.punchline: Both outcomes are framed as wins — the positive because of the baby, the negative because they avoid fighting about the name 'Frisbee' and get to eat disco fries. The absurdity is that the name 'Frisbee' is presented as a serious consideration.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured win-win logic that completely undermines itself. The joke lands on two beats — the absurd baby name 'Frisbee' and then the equally absurd consolation prize of 'disco fries for breakfast 'cause we're sad.' The symmetry of the structure does a lot of work. Criss's breezy optimism is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: I bet it's me. All those years trying to get on 'America's Funniest Home Videos'.
jokes.setup: The pregnancy test is being checked. Criss volunteers that if something is wrong with the result, it's probably his fault.
jokes.punchline: His reasoning is that years of attempting stunts for AFV have presumably damaged his fertility — a completely left-field, absurd non-sequitur that implies a whole offscreen life of failed slapstick ambitions.
jokes.explanation: Quick, odd, and weirdly specific — the AFV detail implies a whole absurd backstory for Criss in two seconds. The joke is in the specificity and the non-sequitur logic. Slightly let down by the vagueness of 'all those years,' but the image it conjures is funny.

jokes.text: Physical comedy reaction: Criss gets hit/scared by something offscreen. 'Aah! Oh! Aah!'
jokes.setup: Criss is speaking when something startles him repeatedly.
jokes.punchline: Three successive yelps imply ongoing slapstick, likely related to the baby or some object nearby. The repeated 'Aah!' escalates the physical reaction into absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that's dependent almost entirely on the visual. In isolation from the transcript, the triple 'Aah!' reads as escalation that works rhythmically but doesn't offer much intellectual comedy. Earns a rewatch bonus because the visual payoff likely enhances it.

jokes.text: It's just not fair. I mean, that guy gets a baby? What kind of idiot gives the little kid orange soda?
jokes.setup: Liz is frustrated watching someone else with a baby, presumably on TV or nearby.
jokes.punchline: Her complaint pivots from existential frustration ('that guy gets a baby?') to a hyper-specific, weirdly mundane parenting critique about orange soda — a classic 30 Rock misdirect.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Liz Lemon joke. She starts big (existential envy about parenthood) and immediately narrows to a trivial, specific grievance (orange soda). The misdirection and character specificity are both strong. This is exactly how Liz operates — her neuroses manifest in granular detail.

jokes.text: Why do you have a baby? Is this a scam? I don't need any scams. I've got a brand-new business selling suicide insurance, and it's going great.
jokes.setup: Dennis Duffy, a known scammer and lowlife, shows up with a baby.
jokes.punchline: He unpromptedly defends himself from accusations of running a scam, then immediately reveals his actual new business is 'suicide insurance' — which is darker and more scam-adjacent than any accusation leveled at him.
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely exceptional joke. Dennis defensively pre-empts scam accusations, then self-incriminates with something far worse — 'suicide insurance.' The phrase is so dark and so perfectly Dennis that it lands hard. His self-assured delivery of a deeply wrong-headed idea is core Dennis Duffy characterization. The economy is excellent: two sentences, two laugh beats. One of the episode's strongest jokes.

jokes.text: And this baby -- This is my adopted son. Obviously, he's gonna be an athlete, so I only got to save up for, like, one year of college.
jokes.setup: Dennis introduces his adopted black son.
jokes.punchline: His 'financial planning' reasoning is that because his son is Black, he'll be an athlete and only need one year of college funding — an appallingly racist assumption delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because it's utterly in character for Dennis — he's oblivious, casually racist, and manages to frame his bigotry as pragmatic financial planning. The show is satirizing this type of person, not endorsing the view. Character integration is near-perfect: no one but Dennis would say this in this way.

jokes.text: You remember Megan Duffy, maiden name Duffy. Hopefully no relation.
jokes.setup: Dennis introduces his wife Megan Duffy.
jokes.punchline: Her maiden name is also Duffy. Dennis adds 'hopefully no relation' as a casual afterthought — implying he may have married a relative and is only mildly concerned about it.
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in comedic economy. Four words — 'hopefully no relation' — do enormous work. The fact that Dennis seems only mildly troubled by possibly marrying a cousin, and the casualness of 'hopefully,' makes this a great joke. Highly quotable, very Dennis, and the structure is airtight: setup (maiden name Duffy), pause, devastatingly understated punchline. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: I recognize you two. Did we have a four-way?
jokes.setup: Dennis looks at Liz and presumably Criss, trying to place them.
jokes.punchline: His method of recognizing people is by checking if he's had group sex with them.
jokes.explanation: Short, punchy, and perfectly in character. Dennis's social mapping of human beings through sexual encounters is a great character beat. Slightly let down by being a well-worn type of joke (the crude non-sequitur), but the specificity of 'four-way' and the earnestness of the delivery elevate it.

jokes.text: No, St. Patty's Day. Remember, honey? / What? It is?
jokes.setup: Dennis tries to jog Megan's memory about meeting Liz and Criss.
jokes.punchline: Megan thinks Dennis is telling her it's St. Patrick's Day, not clarifying how they know these people. Her total confusion implies she has no idea what's going on at any given moment, and Dennis's social world is impenetrably chaotic.
jokes.explanation: A quick misunderstanding beat that's funny because of Megan's complete bewilderment. It's a fast joke that establishes her character efficiently — she is as chaotic and confused as Dennis.

jokes.text: We decided to adopt 'cause Megan's real career-oriented right now, didn't want to wreck her boobs.
jokes.setup: Dennis explains why they adopted instead of having a biological child.
jokes.punchline: The ostensible respect for Megan's career is immediately undercut by the real reason: not wanting to 'wreck her boobs.' Dennis frames misogyny as consideration.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis structure: starts with something that sounds almost reasonable, then reveals the deeply shallow/sexist real motive. The pivot from 'career-oriented' to 'boobs' is perfectly timed and beautifully in character.

jokes.text: His name is Black Dennis? That's racist. / Yeah, right, Liz, the guy with the black son is racist.
jokes.setup: Liz calls out the name 'Black Dennis' as racist.
jokes.punchline: Dennis deflects by pointing out he adopted a black child — as if that makes the racist name impossible. His logic is impeccably wrong and completely sincere.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's counter-logic is perfectly constructed — he uses his own progressive act (interracial adoption) as an ironclad defense against the racist thing he's simultaneously doing. The structure is tight and the irony cuts deep. His absolute confidence makes it land.

jokes.text: Later days, dummies. 21st-century family coming through! This is the new normal!
jokes.setup: Dennis exits with his wife and adopted son.
jokes.punchline: Dennis, one of the most retrograde, offensive characters on television, announces himself as the '21st-century family' and 'the new normal' — the gap between his self-image and reality is enormous.
jokes.explanation: A perfect exit line for Dennis. He's so utterly wrong about what he represents while being so confident about it. 'The new normal' in the mouth of Dennis Duffy is deliciously ironic. Also a meta-joke referencing the NBC show 'The New Normal.'

jokes.text: Yeah. I read the one about a handsome genius who lied to two idiots about reading scripts.
jokes.setup: Dotcom asks Tracy if he's read any of the movie scripts.
jokes.punchline: Tracy describes a fictional script that is actually just a description of what he literally just did — lied about reading scripts. He frames his own deception as a movie premise.
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly self-aware Tracy Jordan joke. He openly confesses to lying by disguising the confession as a movie pitch about himself — and calls himself a 'handsome genius.' The meta quality and the audacity of the self-description work together perfectly.

jokes.text: Dammit-I'll-Pick-A-Name-Later Dotcom Productions.
jokes.setup: Dotcom refers to Tracy's production company.
jokes.punchline: The company name is literally a placeholder — 'Dammit-I'll-Pick-A-Name-Later' — suggesting Tracy never got around to naming it and this has now become the official name.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the specificity of the name itself — 'Dammit-I'll-Pick-A-Name-Later' is the perfect Tracy Jordan company name because it captures his entire approach to responsibility and planning. The hyphenated formality of it as an official name is what makes it excellent.

jokes.text: Okay, it's almost 11:00. Please send in my 8:00.
jokes.setup: Tracy is running pitch meetings. It is noted that it's almost 11:00.
jokes.punchline: Tracy casually asks for his 8:00 appointment — three hours late — with no acknowledgment of or embarrassment about the delay.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly economical Tracy character joke. The three-hour gap between appointment time and actual time is never commented on — the joke is in the casualness. Short and efficient.

jokes.text: While on holiday in Tuscany, a middle-aged divorcée falls in love with a lazy pervert who's into hats.
jokes.setup: A writer is pitching a romantic film to Tracy.
jokes.punchline: The romantic lead is described as 'a lazy pervert who's into hats' — undercuts the Tuscan romance genre instantly. 'Into hats' is the absurd kicker.
jokes.explanation: A tight parody of the 'eat pray love' genre of romantic film that pivots on the hilariously specific descriptor 'lazy pervert who's into hats.' The hat detail is the perfect absurdist kicker — specific enough to feel real, weird enough to be funny.

jokes.text: 'Hitler: The Boy Who Dreamed of Stars!'
jokes.setup: 'In a world with too much freedom, one young man dared to be different.'
jokes.punchline: The inspirational movie trailer language leads to a Hitler biopic — the ultimate subversion of the 'inspirational young man' genre.
jokes.explanation: The structure is near-perfect: the trailer voice-over language is beautifully generic, and 'Hitler: The Boy Who Dreamed of Stars' is the ideal shocking reveal. 'The Boy Who Dreamed of Stars' adds a second layer of ghoulish irony — it sounds warm and aspirational. Strong economy, great structure, high impact.

jokes.text: It's a Harriet Tubman biopic entitled 'The Moses of Maryland'. / I'll buy it! / Sorry, I was talking on my Bluetooth to a guy at the octopus auction. I hate your idea.
jokes.setup: A Harriet Tubman biopic is pitched. Tracy enthusiastically shouts 'I'll buy it!'
jokes.punchline: Tracy reveals he was on Bluetooth talking to someone at an 'octopus auction' — the enthusiasm was for that conversation, not the pitch. 'I hate your idea' is the deadpan reversal.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The misdirection is perfectly executed: the audience (and pitcher) think Tracy is buying the Tubman biopic, and then the rug is pulled with two great reveals stacked — he was on Bluetooth, AND he was at an octopus auction, AND he hates the idea. Three comedic beats in rapid succession. 'Octopus auction' is brilliant absurdist detail. The cold reversal of 'I hate your idea' after such enthusiasm is a perfect button. Earns a high score.

jokes.text: NBC Universal has acquired the film rights to the YouTube clip 'Man Loses Pants on Trampoline'. How would you like to be the voice of Gaboing, the evil wizard who would take jumping away from Jumpland?
jokes.setup: A pitch is being made to Tracy for a film project.
jokes.punchline: The pitch is for a movie based on a silly YouTube clip, featuring an evil wizard named 'Gaboing' in a place called 'Jumpland' — each detail escalating the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: A layered satirical joke about Hollywood IP mining and content-farm filmmaking. Each element is funnier than the last: YouTube clip → film rights → evil wizard named Gaboing → Jumpland. The joke satirizes real studio behavior while building absurdist detail. 'Gaboing' is an excellent made-up word.

jokes.text: Running a movie studio is exhausting. I need a nap. Dotcom, tell us your most interesting story.
jokes.setup: Tracy has just finished pitch meetings.
jokes.punchline: He declares he needs a nap, then immediately asks Dotcom to entertain him — contradicting both the nap plan and the implication that he's too tired for more input.
jokes.explanation: A decent Tracy character beat — his exhaustion evaporates instantly in favor of entertainment. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: I mean, my name has been on adoption lists for years. But Dennis Duffy gets a baby because he's married? It's idiotic.
jokes.setup: Liz vents about the adoption system to Jack.
jokes.punchline: The joke is in the juxtaposition — we've just seen Dennis in full, terrible detail. Liz calling the system that gave HIM a baby 'idiotic' is understated and earned.
jokes.explanation: Works mostly as a callback to the Dennis scene — the audience is nodding along hard because they've just witnessed the full horror of Dennis as a father. The joke is contextual rather than structural.

jokes.text: You know who else was married? Ted Bundy. / I don't think so, Liz. / Really? He's so handsome.
jokes.setup: Liz argues that being married doesn't make someone a good parent and invokes Ted Bundy as an example.
jokes.punchline: Jack says Bundy wasn't married. Liz responds 'Really? He's so handsome' — revealing she only knows Ted Bundy through his notoriously charming public persona and has no idea he was a serial killer.
jokes.explanation: Three-beat joke with a great button. Liz invokes Bundy as a smart rhetorical point, Jack corrects her, and then Liz's response reveals total ignorance — she's drawn to his appearance rather than horrified by his crimes. 'Is he still alive?' would have been the kicker but 'He's so handsome' is better — funnier and more specific to Liz's character.

jokes.text: Is he still alive?
jokes.setup: After saying Ted Bundy is handsome, Liz genuinely asks if he's still alive.
jokes.punchline: Liz doesn't know who Ted Bundy is well enough to know he was executed in 1989 — she's asking about a serial killer like she's asking about a celebrity crush.
jokes.explanation: The follow-up kicker to the Bundy joke. 'Is he still alive?' as a genuine question about a serial killer is a great button — maximum economy (four words), extends the previous joke's impact. Works as a standalone beat too.

jokes.text: I ignore it when you eat popsicles by biting them with your teeth, which is insane!
jokes.setup: Liz is making the case that she and Criss are as committed as a married couple.
jokes.punchline: Her example of commitment and sacrifice is tolerating his popsicle-eating method — an absurdly trivial grievance elevated to the level of profound sacrifice.
jokes.explanation: This is Liz Lemon at her most specific and most herself. The joke works because biting popsicles with your teeth IS a legitimately controversial thing, and Liz elevating it to the level of marital devotion is perfect. 'Which is insane!' is a great button. High character integration — this is a uniquely Liz grievance.

jokes.text: Me need piece of paper to know how I feel! Guhhhh, Liz marry Criss? Doy! Errr, all right.
jokes.setup: After agreeing to get married, Liz mocks the idea of needing a marriage certificate to legitimize their relationship.
jokes.punchline: She does a caveman impression of herself — 'Me need piece of paper' — satirizing the institution even while agreeing to participate in it.
jokes.explanation: A funny self-deprecating moment where Liz performs her own intellectual resistance to an institution she's about to embrace. The caveman voice is a physical comedy beat. Character-specific and charming, but not structurally exceptional.

jokes.text: We'll get a license today, get married tomorrow, blammo! Engaged!
jokes.setup: Liz describes her casual plan for getting married.
jokes.punchline: The word 'blammo' as her expression of matrimonial enthusiasm, followed by announcing they're 'engaged' AFTER already deciding to get married — she has the process backwards.
jokes.explanation: The charm is in 'blammo' and the backwards engagement logic. Liz's complete disregard for romantic convention is funny and in character.

jokes.text: 'Top Gun'-style. / Jenna Maroney, you are my slave.
jokes.setup: Someone says 'Top Gun'-style as a transition/reference, and then Jack (or another character) gravely informs Jenna: 'You are my slave.'
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition of the 'Top Gun' bro-culture reference immediately followed by the medieval/absurd declaration of slavery is a jarring and funny transition.
jokes.explanation: Works as an abrupt comedic gear-shift. The absurdity of the slavery claim is the real joke; 'Top Gun-style' is a setup misdirect.

jokes.text: What? But the sheik who won me in that poker game was beheaded.
jokes.setup: Jenna is told she is someone's slave.
jokes.punchline: Her objection is not 'I can't be a slave' but rather that the previous sheik who owned her was beheaded — implying a whole history of Jenna being wagered in card games and changing ownership.
jokes.explanation: A brilliant piece of implied backstory comedy. Jenna doesn't question the institution of being owned — she just has a procedural objection about ownership transfer. The casual mention of a 'sheik who won me in a poker game' being beheaded packs multiple jokes into one sentence. Perfectly Jenna — she treats her own dehumanization as a minor administrative inconvenience.

jokes.text: No, do you remember in 1994 you made a commercial for Surge Cola? For 100 Surge points, I got these shades! / Oh, yeah? For 500 Surge points, I got this leather jacket!
jokes.setup: Terry explains how he came to own Jenna — through a Surge Cola points redemption commercial from 1994.
jokes.punchline: Jack and Terry have a one-upmanship exchange about Surge points prizes, with Jack triumphantly revealing his leather jacket was worth 500 points — the two men bonding over this absurd 90s loyalty program.
jokes.explanation: The 90s Surge Cola world-building is funny and specific — Surge was a real hyper-caffeinated soda, which grounds the absurdity. Jack and Terry's genuine enthusiasm for their prizes (shades and a leather jacket) is a great comic beat. The escalation structure works well.

jokes.text: For a million points, he got me! Surge! Suck it down!
jokes.setup: Jack and Terry are comparing Surge Cola prizes.
jokes.punchline: Jenna reveals she was the million-point prize, complete with what sounds like the ad's slogan ('Surge! Suck it down!'). She was literally a commercial prize.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Jenna was literally the million-point prize is a great comedic escalation. 'Surge! Suck it down!' as a non-sequitur slogan delivery is excellent. Her complete unselfconsciousness about having been a commercial commodity is perfectly Jenna. The escalation from shades (100pts) → jacket (500pts) → human being (1M pts) has beautiful structure.

jokes.text: My boyfriend was supposed to pick me up after that shoot, so I called him, and I was like, 'O.J., where are you?' And he was like, 'Wait, you're alive? Then who did I kill?'
jokes.setup: Jenna is reminiscing about the Surge commercial shoot in 1994.
jokes.punchline: She casually reveals her boyfriend at the time was O.J. Simpson, and recreates a conversation where O.J. is confused about who he murdered — because apparently he was expecting it to be Jenna.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is exceptional: sets up an apparently normal 'where are you' call, then pivots to O.J.'s response which contains two dark implications stacked — he expected Jenna to be dead, and he's confused about who he DID kill. The joke treats one of the most notorious murders in American history as a casual plot point in Jenna's love life. Dark, specific, perfectly structured. 'Then who did I kill?' is an all-timer line.

jokes.text: Well, you do have the wind-battered face of a New England cod fisherman, if that's what you're asking.
jokes.setup: Liz asks Jack if she looks 'positively glowing.'
jokes.punchline: Jack affirms she does look a particular way — but that way is 'the wind-battered face of a New England cod fisherman.'
jokes.explanation: A masterful insult joke. Jack answers Liz's question technically honestly — yes, she does look a particular way — but the descriptor is devastating and absurdly specific. 'Wind-battered face of a New England cod fisherman' is an extraordinary image. The 'if that's what you're asking' button is perfect deadpan. One of the episode's top jokes. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: To Criss, right? This isn't one of those Internet marriage scams where they prey on the elderly?
jokes.setup: Jack responds to news of Liz's upcoming marriage with enthusiasm, then immediately adds a caveat.
jokes.punchline: Jack's first instinct upon hearing Liz is getting married is to verify it isn't an elder-care scam — both insulting Liz and revealing his worldview that such things happen routinely.
jokes.explanation: Jack's concern about an 'Internet marriage scam that preys on the elderly' is a great character joke — it simultaneously patronizes Liz and reveals Jack's paranoid WASP worldview. Clean and well-delivered.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. This is the best hug I've ever had. / I know.
jokes.setup: Jack gives Liz a hug after she announces she's getting married.
jokes.punchline: Liz's amazed declaration that it's the best hug she's ever had, confirmed by Jack with zero irony.
jokes.explanation: A sweet character beat that's funny because of Jack's complete agreement — 'I know' suggests he has spent considerable time optimizing his hugging. Works on the Liz/Jack relationship level.

jokes.text: I'll get Tony Bennett to sing. I saved his life at an illegal pai gow game once. He owes me a favor.
jokes.setup: Jack immediately begins planning an elaborate wedding for Liz.
jokes.punchline: His connection to Tony Bennett is through saving his life at an 'illegal pai gow game' — the specific game (pai gow is an obscure gambling game) and the life-saving detail combine into a perfect Jack Donaghy backstory.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully specific Jack Donaghy world-building. 'Illegal pai gow game' is the perfect choice of backstory — it's exotic, vaguely criminal, and exactly the kind of thing Jack would casually reference. That Tony Bennett owes Jack a life debt from it is peak Jack.

jokes.text: No, I can't. I got rid of that after Hurricane Irene. I had forgotten to stock up on toilet paper, but I had remembered to stock up on seven-layer dip --
jokes.setup: Jack mentions Liz's wedding dress.
jokes.punchline: Liz explains she used the dress (presumably as toilet paper) during Hurricane Irene because she had stocked seven-layer dip but not actual toilet paper.
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Liz Lemon. She prepared for a hurricane by stocking party dip instead of necessities, and sacrificed her wedding dress to compensate. The specificity of 'seven-layer dip' (not just 'dip') is a key detail that makes it great. The implication is left to the audience, which is the right comedic choice.

jokes.text: Sol Rosenbear and I would like to thank everyone for coming to our destination wedding here on the Love Boat. Unfortunately, Sol has discovered my previous relationship with Gopher, so he will be seeking an annulment once we reach Puerto Vallarta.
jokes.setup: Jack asks if Liz ever dreamed about her wedding as a little girl. We get a cutaway.
jokes.punchline: Young Liz is playing wedding with a teddy bear (Sol Rosenbear) on the Love Boat, and the marriage is already dissolving due to her previous affair with Gopher (a character from The Love Boat). The dream wedding involves celebrity TV characters, destination drama, and an immediate annulment.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional. The name 'Sol Rosenbear' alone is a great joke (Jewish teddy bear husband). The child Liz's wedding fantasy is already a disaster — on the Love Boat, with a Love Boat character affair as the complication. The formality of the announcement ('we would like to thank everyone for coming') contrasted with the immediate dissolution makes it perfect. It says everything about Liz as a character — even her childhood wedding fantasy was neurotic and doomed. One of the episode's best moments.

jokes.text: I realized a long time ago that weddings aren't about love. They're just a giant industry that preys on gender stereotypes to make adult women spend a ton of money and act like selfish children!
jokes.setup: Liz explains her position on weddings to Jack.
jokes.punchline: The irony is that even as she makes this speech, she is clearly emotionally invested in her own wedding — the rant itself is somewhat unhinged, and will be immediately undercut by her mother storming in.
jokes.explanation: A functional character beat that sets up the running irony of Liz secretly wanting a special day. The writing is competent but the sentiment isn't particularly novel — feminist wedding critique has been done. Works in context.

jokes.text: Maybe there's not gonna be a wedding! / You're ruining my special day! / Mom, what the [beep] are you wearing?
jokes.setup: Liz is ranting that she doesn't want a special day or wedding. Her mother suddenly appears.
jokes.punchline: Liz's mom immediately declares Liz is 'ruining my special day' — making it about herself. Then Liz pivots to commenting on her mom's outfit with a bleep, completely derailing the scene.
jokes.explanation: Three-beat joke: Liz's anti-wedding declaration → mom's self-centered reversal → Liz's startled non-sequitur about the outfit. The mom stealing 'my special day' is the main joke, and it lands. The bleeping suggests a visual that's apparently shocking enough to produce profanity.

jokes.text: I remember when Bravo used to air operas. / I reject the wedding industry's phallocentric fairy tale grotesquerie!
jokes.setup: Liz's mom arrives and the wedding topic is in play.
jokes.punchline: Jack's mild nostalgic comment about Bravo's programming history is immediately overwhelmed by Liz's mom declaring she 'rejects the phallocentric fairy tale grotesquerie' — the vocabulary is hilariously academic for the context.
jokes.explanation: 'Phallocentric fairy tale grotesquerie' is a great phrase — it's the kind of academic feminist language that would come from a certain type of 1970s woman. Jack's gentle Bravo callback is a nice contrast. 'Grotesquerie' alone is worth points.

jokes.text: So tomorrow Liz Lemon is getting married in a sweatshirt, no bra!
jokes.setup: Liz declares she'll have a no-frills wedding as a feminist statement.
jokes.punchline: Her mom enthusiastically announces the plan as if it's an achievement — 'sweatshirt, no bra' — as a declaration of feminist triumph, not realizing (or not caring) that this is embarrassing for her daughter.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'sweatshirt, no bra' as the pinnacle of her mom's feminist vision is funny. The mom's pride in announcing this is the joke.

jokes.text: Oh, for God's sakes, Lemon, don't take a stand about your own wedding. Think about that kid you're trying to adopt. What will you tell him if he asks to see pictures?
jokes.setup: Liz announces her plan to get married in a sweatshirt.
jokes.punchline: Jack's pragmatic argument against the sweatshirt wedding is concern about future adoption photo evidence — a practical, slightly cold reframe of the sentimental question.
jokes.explanation: Jack's instinct to reframe emotional decisions as practical image management is a strong character beat. The question of what to tell the adopted child about wedding photos is a funny and slightly sad angle.

jokes.text: I will tell her or if that I took an amazing stand against the wedding industrial complex. We are registered at Popcorn Palace!
jokes.setup: Jack suggests Liz think about her future adopted child's perspective on wedding photos.
jokes.punchline: Liz's defiant response invokes the 'wedding industrial complex' as a serious political stance, then undermines it by announcing they're 'registered at Popcorn Palace' — the most un-serious possible gift registry.
jokes.explanation: 'Popcorn Palace' as a wedding registry is a great joke — it's both completely in character for Liz and perfectly undercuts her rhetorical stance. The phrase 'wedding industrial complex' is funny because it's a slightly absurd application of the 'military-industrial complex' framing. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: All right, now that I'm finished with my handwriting sample for the FBI, let's look at your test results.
jokes.setup: Dr. Spaceman transitions to Tracy's insurance physical results.
jokes.punchline: He casually mentions he's just completed a handwriting sample for the FBI as if this is completely normal — implying he's under investigation, which is fully in character for Dr. Leo Spaceman.
jokes.explanation: Pure Dr. Spaceman. He has apparently just finished providing evidence to federal investigators as a casual pre-appointment task. The casualness is everything — 'now that I'm finished with my handwriting sample for the FBI' delivered with complete nonchalance. One of the cleanest character jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Oh, this is puzzling, Tracy. There doesn't seem to be anything wrong with you at all. / What? / I guess we've replaced so much of you over the years that you're maybe not you anymore, but you're healthy.
jokes.setup: Dr. Spaceman delivers Tracy's physical results.
jokes.punchline: The 'good news' is delivered as if it's bad news, then explained with the revelation that Tracy has been so extensively repaired that he may not technically be himself anymore — a Ship of Theseus joke applied to a celebrity body.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever joke with real philosophical depth. 'You're maybe not you anymore, but you're healthy' applies the Ship of Theseus paradox to Tracy Jordan's body through a lifetime of medical procedures. That this is presented as possibly bad news makes it funnier. Dr. Spaceman's baffled delivery of good news as puzzling is perfect.

jokes.text: I always assumed I'd die young because, you know, I look so much like James Dean. And that gave me the freedom to live without consequences!
jokes.setup: Tracy reacts badly to good health news.
jokes.punchline: Tracy has constructed his entire philosophy of consequence-free living on the belief that he looks like James Dean and will therefore die young. The confidence of the James Dean comparison is the first joke; the logical structure built on it is the second.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's life philosophy being built on an absurd physical comparison to James Dean is characteristically excellent. The logic — 'I look like him, he died young, therefore I will too' — is beautifully Tracy. This is high character integration: no other character on TV would construct this rationale.

jokes.text: That's why I'm always breaking the law, buying exotic sharks, forgetting to feed them, and then trying to hug them!
jokes.setup: Tracy explains the behaviors his 'live without consequences' philosophy enabled.
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from generic lawbreaking to exotic shark ownership, to neglect, to the absurd conclusion of trying to hug the neglected sharks.
jokes.explanation: This is outstanding. The list structure is perfectly calibrated: 'breaking the law' (generic) → 'buying exotic sharks' (specific and alarming) → 'forgetting to feed them' (darkly negligent) → 'trying to hug them' (the absurd, dangerous, deeply Tracy conclusion). The escalation is masterful. 'Trying to hug them' as the culminating irresponsible act is inspired. One of the episode's top jokes.

jokes.text: How many years, Dr. Spaceman? / 40. Maybe 50. / I'm sorry.
jokes.setup: Tracy asks how many years he has left to live.
jokes.punchline: Dr. Spaceman gives a perfectly healthy prognosis (40-50 years), then immediately apologizes for it — treating longevity as bad news requiring condolences.
jokes.explanation: Exquisite economy. 'I'm sorry' after delivering a 40-50 year life expectancy is the perfectly devastating button. Three words do enormous work. The inversion of doctor/patient dynamics (apologizing for good health) is the joke, and it's executed with maximum efficiency.

jokes.text: Look, I'm not happy about this either. The money I've made off your health problems has put me almost all the way through medical school.
jokes.setup: Dr. Spaceman commiserates with Tracy over the healthy diagnosis.
jokes.punchline: Dr. Spaceman reveals he has been profiting from Tracy's medical problems AND that he's not yet finished with medical school — meaning he's been practicing medicine without a full degree.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional television comedy — potentially the episode's best joke. It works on multiple levels: (1) Spaceman is financially invested in Tracy's illness, (2) he's actively treating a patient while not yet having finished medical school, (3) his commiseration is entirely self-interested. The phrase 'almost all the way through medical school' is the killer detail — it's not that he dropped out, he's simply not done yet. The character integration is near-perfect: this is exactly what Dr. Spaceman is. Comparable to the anchor '8.0' example in impact; arguably exceeds it.

jokes.text: I'm gonna have to start living like there's a tomorrow. Open an IRA. Brush my teeth. Drink eight glasses a day of that stuff. You know, clear bathtub juice.
jokes.setup: Tracy bemoans that he now has to take responsibility for his life.
jokes.punchline: His list of responsible adult activities culminates in 'drink eight glasses a day of that stuff — clear bathtub juice.' Tracy doesn't know the word 'water.'
jokes.explanation: 'Clear bathtub juice' is one of the most memorable jokes in the episode — Tracy Jordan's term for water. The list structure (IRA → teeth → water) escalates to the absurd. The specificity of 'bathtub juice' (not just 'clear stuff') and the reasoning behind it (he genuinely doesn't know what water is called) is brilliantly Tracy. This is a top-tier joke.

jokes.text: Tracy, I'm afraid I don't have a pamphlet to help you get through this. But I do have a pamphlet that has a bunch of drawings of vaginae. / I'll take it.
jokes.setup: Dr. Spaceman tries to offer Tracy emotional guidance materials.
jokes.punchline: He doesn't have a relevant pamphlet but offers a completely unrelated gynecological pamphlet, which Tracy immediately accepts without hesitation.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical two-character joke. The absurdist detail of a doctor having a pamphlet of vagina drawings available for distribution is funny. Tracy's immediate and unqualified 'I'll take it' is the perfect button — he has no interest in emotional guidance but is immediately on board for the other thing. The Latin plural 'vaginae' from Spaceman adds an unexpected academic touch.

jokes.text: I'm moving to Arizona to be with my new slave master Terry to live in a birdcage he built.
jokes.setup: Jenna explains her reasons for wanting out of her TGS contract.
jokes.punchline: Her reason for leaving is to 'live in a birdcage' built by her slave master — presented with complete normalcy as a career decision.
jokes.explanation: The matter-of-fact delivery of 'a birdcage he built' as a selling point is funny. Jenna's complete comfort with deeply abnormal arrangements is consistent with her character.

jokes.text: Now, Terry, I suspect you know it's illegal for someone to own another human being.
jokes.setup: Jack addresses Terry's claim to own Jenna.
jokes.punchline: Jack's perfectly calibrated corporate-lawyer tone applied to 'it's illegal to own a human being' — treating slavery as a business negotiation matter.
jokes.explanation: Jack's measured corporate response to slavery as a contract dispute is darkly funny. 'I suspect you know' is perfect — polite, lawyer-y, and slightly condescending.

jokes.text: And thanks to decades of partying, Jenna's internal organs will get you nothing on the black market.
jokes.setup: Jack and others are calculating Jenna's monetary value.
jokes.punchline: Among the depreciating assets: her organs are worthless on the black market due to lifestyle damage.
jokes.explanation: The black market organ valuation is a darkly funny corporate devaluation metric. The specificity of 'decades of partying' as the cause is perfectly Jenna.

jokes.text: A 7th-grade education, hepatitis D, bullet in jaw, fatwa, credit card debt, wanted by the Yakuza -- Jenna Maroney is worth... $2,000.
jokes.setup: Jack lists Jenna's liabilities to calculate her worth.
jokes.punchline: The list of increasingly dramatic liabilities (hepatitis D, bullet in jaw, fatwa, Yakuza) culminates in a verdict of $2,000 — the comic contrast between the scale of her problems and the pathetically small valuation.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalating list comedy. 'Hepatitis D' (not a real strain — the escalation past C is a joke in itself), 'bullet in jaw,' 'fatwa,' and 'wanted by the Yakuza' form a perfect comedic list, with the pause and dramatic reveal of '$2,000' as the devastating punchline. The gap between the list and the number is the joke. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Daddy, why are you doing this?
jokes.setup: Jack is systematically devaluing Jenna in front of her 'slave master.'
jokes.punchline: Jenna calls Jack 'Daddy' — revealing her emotional dependence on Jack as a father figure at this moment of vulnerability.
jokes.explanation: A one-word (almost) joke — 'Daddy' as a term of address for Jack in this specific moment is both funny and a little sad. Great economy and strong character integration for Jenna.

jokes.text: Fine. In Arizona, two grand will buy me a castle and a pillowcase full of meth.
jokes.setup: Terry is told Jenna is worth $2,000.
jokes.punchline: He immediately reframes $2,000 as enormous purchasing power in Arizona — a 'castle' and a 'pillowcase full of meth.' The pillowcase is the perfect absurdist unit of measurement.
jokes.explanation: A great joke on Arizona's cost of living AND meth culture. 'Pillowcase full of meth' is an inspired unit — specific enough to be funny, suggests someone who thinks of drug quantities in household containers. The castle/meth pairing is absurdly specific.

jokes.text: Make it out to 'Doomsday Enterprises'.
jokes.setup: A check is being written to pay Terry off.
jokes.punchline: The company name is 'Doomsday Enterprises' — implying Terry's slave-owning, Arizona-castle-dwelling, meth-buying operation is formally incorporated under a name suggesting apocalyptic intent.
jokes.explanation: Economy joke — the name 'Doomsday Enterprises' does all the work. It's the perfect corporate vehicle for a man who owns people and builds birdcages.

jokes.text: I used to only say stuff like that in my white nerd voice.
jokes.setup: Tracy has just delivered a line about 'greatest probability of succeeding in the global marketplace' — business-speak that sounds unlike him.
jokes.punchline: He acknowledges the voice shift and implies he has a 'white nerd voice' he deploys for certain contexts — and that running a studio has mainstreamed it.
jokes.explanation: A self-aware character beat that works as both meta-comedy (Tracy acknowledging his own verbal register shift) and as a character development joke about what studio ownership is doing to him. 'White nerd voice' is a great, specific phrase.

jokes.text: Jeez, I feel like we're at a deli. / Deli? Save it for the honeymoon.
jokes.setup: At the Marriage Bureau, they're taking numbered tickets like a deli.
jokes.punchline: Criss makes a pun on 'deli' — presumably referencing 'deli-ghted' or the honeymoon context, though the joke may be a double entendre about a deli counter's associations.
jokes.explanation: A quick wordplay beat that works as a mild pun. The 'save it for the honeymoon' deflection is charming but the joke is thin. Functional filler.

jokes.text: Okay, you take our paperwork to the clerk because black women love you. / Oh! I see you over there, you little gumdrop. Don't hide from Shanice! / I'll give you a bath in the sink like a baby!
jokes.setup: Liz sends Criss to deal with the clerk, citing his appeal to 'black women.'
jokes.punchline: The clerk (Shanice) immediately validates this with an overwhelming display of affection — calling him a 'gumdrop' and threatening a sink bath.
jokes.explanation: 'Don't hide from Shanice!' and 'I'll give you a bath in the sink like a baby!' are great over-the-top affection lines. The joke rewards Liz's cynical strategy immediately and extravagantly.

jokes.text: We'll get married and magically become amazing parents! Just like the Hiltons!
jokes.setup: Liz enthusiastically explains their plan.
jokes.punchline: 'Just like the Hiltons' is the ironic comparison — the Hilton family being most famous for Paris Hilton rather than exemplary parenting.
jokes.explanation: A functional celebrity reference joke. The irony is clear but the joke relies entirely on cultural knowledge of the Hiltons' parenting reputation. Decent but not inventive.

jokes.text: You really didn't invite anyone to your wedding? / No, I mean, who cares, right? We're at City Hall. You guys are wearing Mets t-shirts -- / Yeah, 'cause we were wearing them when we first -- / Met. / Met. / My God, you're beautiful. / This is the greatest day of my life.
jokes.setup: Liz and Criss are asking strangers in Mets t-shirts to be their witnesses. The strangers reveal they're wearing the shirts because they were wearing them when they first met.
jokes.punchline: Liz starts to finish their story ('Mets t-shirts because...') and both Liz and the stranger simultaneously say 'Met' — a triple pun (Mets/met/met). One stranger is so moved they declare it 'the greatest day of my life.'
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed wordplay moment. Mets → met is a natural pun, but the simultaneous delivery and the emotional reaction ('My God, you're beautiful. This is the greatest day of my life.') from a total stranger elevate it to something genuinely sweet and funny. The structure is tight and the payoff is well-earned.

jokes.text: You okay? / Yeah. I just thought there'd be more people here in gym clothes, carrying bags full of toilet paper.
jokes.setup: They're waiting at City Hall and Liz seems unsettled.
jokes.punchline: Liz's vision of a City Hall wedding involved people in gym clothes with toilet paper bags — a specific and telling picture of what she expected her future to look like.
jokes.explanation: A quietly great Liz Lemon moment. 'Gym clothes and bags full of toilet paper' as the expected City Hall demographic speaks to her low expectations for her own life circumstances. Specific and character-true.

jokes.text: You know, I always imagined getting married right when they take your picture on Splash Mountain.
jokes.setup: Criss says 'we don't have to do it this way' and mentions his imagined wedding.
jokes.punchline: His dream wedding venue is the photo moment on Splash Mountain at Disney World — the most casually absurd, un-romantic setting imaginable, delivered with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully specific and absurd. Splash Mountain as a wedding venue works because the photo moment is genuinely romantic in its spontaneity — but also extremely undignified. Criss's sincere delivery of this as a cherished dream is perfect. It tells you everything about him.

jokes.text: The first wedding I ever went to, I was a flower girl for my Aunt Linda. When they said, 'You may now kiss the bride,' I did my first ever eye-roll.
jokes.setup: Liz explains her complicated relationship with weddings.
jokes.punchline: As a child flower girl, her reaction to 'you may kiss the bride' was not joy but her 'first ever eye-roll' — establishing her fundamental skepticism as a primal, congenital trait.
jokes.explanation: The detail of the 'first ever eye-roll' is wonderful — Liz's entire personality condensed into a childhood anecdote. The idea that she discovered the eye-roll at a wedding is perfect character origin mythology. High character integration.

jokes.text: And today, I honor that little girl's eye-roll with this masterpiece. / [Visual gag: Liz in a sweatshirt at City Hall as her wedding outfit]
jokes.setup: Liz declares she'll honor her childhood cynicism.
jokes.punchline: She calls her sweatshirt-at-City-Hall wedding a 'masterpiece' — the gap between the word and the reality is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The visual payoff of Liz in a sweatshirt declaring it a 'masterpiece' works as a callback and a visual gag. The irony of 'masterpiece' for this outfit is solid.

jokes.text: Great. 'Cause I forgot my birth certificate.
jokes.setup: Liz delivers her moving speech about honoring her eye-roll with this 'masterpiece' of a minimal wedding.
jokes.punchline: Criss's response is a completely flat practical problem: he forgot his birth certificate.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic deflation. Liz's big emotional moment is punctured instantly by a mundane logistical failure. The economy is excellent — five words max comedy.

jokes.text: Are you kidding me, Chros?
jokes.setup: Criss reveals he forgot his birth certificate.
jokes.punchline: Liz calls him 'Chros' — apparently a nickname/insult, or a mispronunciation of 'Criss,' implying she degrades his name when angry.
jokes.explanation: The name 'Chros' is a funny detail — her frustration manifests in a garbled version of his name. A quick, funny character beat.

jokes.text: And even though Shanice said she'd let it slide if I sat on her hand --
jokes.setup: Criss explains how he tried to resolve the missing birth certificate situation.
jokes.punchline: Shanice (the clerk) offered to overlook it if Criss sat on her hand — a deeply inappropriate workplace proposition delivered as a straightforward negotiating condition.
jokes.explanation: A perfect payoff to the Shanice running gag. Her workplace harassment escalates naturally from 'sink bath' to physical demands, and Criss reporting it as a neutral bureaucratic negotiation is great.

jokes.text: Lemon, I haven't seen anything in the news about attitudes towards marriage changing forever because of one brave woman.
jokes.setup: Jack calls Liz, presumably to check in after she left.
jokes.punchline: Jack mocks Liz's self-important stance about making a statement with her casual wedding — the news has not been changed by her sweatshirt protest.
jokes.explanation: A pointed Jack Donaghy callback that punctures Liz's self-mythology elegantly. His delivery of 'one brave woman' is rich with sarcasm.

jokes.text: Oh, also, I told him you're Italian, so he might call you Tina --
jokes.setup: Jack mentions he e-mailed Tony Bennett about singing at Liz's wedding.
jokes.punchline: He told Tony Bennett that Liz is Italian (she isn't) and apparently gave her the name 'Tina,' creating a false identity for Liz that Tony Bennett now believes.
jokes.explanation: A funny extension of the Tony Bennett gag — Jack has already created an elaborate false identity for Liz. The 'might call you Tina' as a casual afterthought is well-delivered.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah! Oh, you can walk away from me all day, you little tiger cub! Raar!
jokes.setup: Criss apparently walks away from the clerk window.
jokes.punchline: Shanice calls after him as 'tiger cub' and makes a 'Raar!' sound — escalating her workplace harassment to animal roleplay.
jokes.explanation: The Shanice running gag is escalating well. 'Tiger cub' and 'Raar!' are funny additions. The running gag structure rewards attentive viewers.

jokes.text: I work at the Marriage Bureau, but I'll never get married.
jokes.setup: A brief aside from a Marriage Bureau employee.
jokes.punchline: A dry, melancholy confession that functions as an ironic character beat — the person who processes marriages for others is entirely without romantic prospects.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully economical throwaway joke. One line, perfect irony, maximum efficiency. The bleakness is the joke.

jokes.text: I didn't want anyone to see me like this, she lied.
jokes.setup: Jenna is upset about her $2,000 valuation and Jack comes to comfort her.
jokes.punchline: Jenna says 'I didn't want anyone to see me like this' — but adds 'she lied' as a self-narrated tag, acknowledging she absolutely wanted to be seen.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Jenna narrating her own lie in the third person with 'she lied' is a perfect meta-comedy moment. It requires no setup beyond knowing Jenna's character — she is constitutionally incapable of not performing her emotions. The self-aware self-deception is brilliantly executed. Highly quotable, extremely Jenna.

jokes.text: $2,000, Jack? I've stolen more than that from my cleaning lady's purse!
jokes.setup: Jenna is upset about her valuation.
jokes.punchline: Her frame of reference for '$2,000' is that she's stolen more than that from her cleaning lady — both establishing her wealth and her casual criminality toward employees.
jokes.explanation: A great Jenna joke. The indignation is funny, the comparison is funnier, and the casual admission of repeatedly stealing from her cleaning lady is the dark kicker. High economy and character integration.

jokes.text: In this market, $2,000 is more than respectable. I mean, look at Kenneth. He's worth $5 tops. / I'm gonna hold you to that, sir!
jokes.setup: Jack tries to reassure Jenna that $2,000 is a reasonable valuation.
jokes.punchline: He uses Kenneth as a lower benchmark — worth '$5 tops.' Kenneth's response ('I'm gonna hold you to that, sir!') treats this as a compliment or promise rather than an insult.
jokes.explanation: A great two-character joke. Kenneth's '$5' valuation is perfectly in character for his selfless, almost inhuman simplicity — and his response ('I'm gonna hold you to that, sir!') is the perfect Kenneth reaction, treating the insult as either a promise or a compliment. Both characters are absolutely true to themselves.

jokes.text: I've been divorced twice. I'm at an age where I no longer need erectile softeners. I'm number two at an American television company, with no possibility for promotion. I'll probably die on this job. I've already had one heart attack.
jokes.setup: Jack tries to cheer Jenna up by relating his own decline.
jokes.punchline: The list of Jack's personal failings escalates grimly — culminating in the darkly funny 'I'll probably die on this job,' and the already-established heart attack. 'Erectile softeners' instead of 'erectile dysfunction medication' is the unexpected detail.
jokes.explanation: Jack's self-pity list is funny because of both the content and the delivery — 'no longer need erectile softeners' is a euphemistic inversion (softeners vs. enhancers) that's darkly funny. 'I'll probably die on this job' lands as sincere and grim. Strong character work.

jokes.text: I used to be a young man with promise. I coined the phrase, 'You wish, pal!'
jokes.setup: Jack continues his self-pity speech about his decline.
jokes.punchline: His crowning youthful achievement is claiming he coined the phrase 'You wish, pal!' — an utterly generic, unmemorable catchphrase presented as a genuine cultural contribution.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. 'You wish, pal!' is chosen specifically because it's the least impressive catchphrase imaginable — generic, unmemorable, not even mildly clever. Jack presenting this as a genuine legacy is both a great character joke and a good structural subversion.

jokes.text: Oh, God. I'm worth less than you.
jokes.setup: Jack has listed all his failures to make Jenna feel better.
jokes.punchline: Jack's moment of self-realization: by his own argument, he has talked himself into being worth less than a $2,000 actress.
jokes.explanation: A clean logical conclusion to the self-pity speech. Jack arrives at a devastating self-assessment through his own argument — and Jenna's delighted response ('Oh! Thank you, Jack!') is the perfect button.

jokes.text: What are you doing? Why did you change your clothes? / Well, this is what I was wearing when we met in Riverside Park. Remember? You said, 'Nice turtleneck'. / No, I said, 'Nice turtleneck.' / Thank you again!
jokes.setup: Criss has changed into a turtleneck. Liz is confused. He explains it's what he wore when they first met.
jokes.punchline: Liz says she said 'Nice turtleneck' (sarcastically), Criss says she said 'Nice turtleneck' (genuinely), and he responds 'Thank you again!' — he received the original sarcasm as a sincere compliment and is thanking her again for it years later.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed tonal joke — the same words ('Nice turtleneck') mean opposite things depending on delivery, and Criss received the sarcastic version as genuine. 'Thank you again!' is a perfect button that retroactively reframes their entire relationship origin story.

jokes.text: Great, so now you're more dressed up than I am at my own wedding. But whatever. I got witnesses. These guys were in the park either fighting or having sex.
jokes.setup: Liz returns with witnesses she found in the park.
jokes.punchline: She introduces them as people who were 'either fighting or having sex' — she couldn't tell which, and didn't ask for clarification before recruiting them.
jokes.explanation: The casual 'either fighting or having sex' with no preference expressed and no follow-up questions asked is a perfect Liz Lemon detail. The indifference to which it was, combined with recruiting them anyway, is very funny.

jokes.text: Of course, it had to be someone with nothing to do on a Wednesday afternoon.
jokes.setup: Liz sees that the surprise witness Criss found is someone unexpected.
jokes.punchline: Her pre-emption of the reveal — 'it had to be someone with nothing to do on a Wednesday afternoon' — is a great setup for whoever is about to walk in.
jokes.explanation: A functional setup line for the Dennis reveal. Works as a joke beat in isolation but is mostly scaffolding.

jokes.text: No, no, no, you didn't. / Mazel tov, dummies. You're Jewish, right, Liz?
jokes.setup: The surprise witness is revealed to be Dennis Duffy.
jokes.punchline: Dennis greets them with 'Mazel tov, dummies' — his characteristically tone-deaf attempt at cultural sensitivity ('you're Jewish, right, Liz?') in the same breath as calling them 'dummies.'
jokes.explanation: The episode title joke lands perfectly. 'Mazel tov, dummies' is a brilliant phrase that encapsulates Dennis entirely — simultaneously attempting cultural respect and casual insult. The follow-up 'you're Jewish, right, Liz?' delivered as he's already said it is perfect Dennis timing. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: I don't know! It's not the most important day of my life! Getting my show picked up, or meeting you, or the time I got a sleeve of Starburst with all pink! Those were all more important days!
jokes.setup: Liz and Criss are arguing about whether the wedding is important.
jokes.punchline: Liz lists events more important than her wedding, culminating in 'the time I got a sleeve of Starburst with all pink' — placing the TV pickup and meeting her fiancé above the wedding, but at least the candy is up there too.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalation structure is excellent: TV show pickup → meeting Criss → all-pink Starburst sleeve. The candy is the kicker and it's perfect — pink Starburst being universally the best flavor makes this specific and true, while its placement alongside genuinely major life events is perfectly Liz Lemon. This is character comedy at its finest.

jokes.text: Because I'm Liz Lemon! My parents spent the money they saved up for my wedding on a PT Cruiser.
jokes.setup: Liz explains her emotional state about the wedding.
jokes.punchline: Her parents spent her wedding fund on a PT Cruiser — a car famous for being unloved and mocked. The specificity of the PT Cruiser (not just 'a car') is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The PT Cruiser is inspired — it's a car associated with regret and dubious taste, which adds a layer of insult to the injury of having her parents spend the money on it. Very specific, very Lemon family.

jokes.text: Ergo. Affleck's finally gonna get that Oscar.
jokes.setup: Liz uses 'ergo' in her emotional speech about not caring about the wedding.
jokes.punchline: Criss notices 'ergo' and makes a completely off-topic Ben Affleck Oscar reference — his train of thought derailed by one word.
jokes.explanation: Criss makes an Affleck-Oscar joke as an interruption joke — presumably a reference to 'Argo' (which won Best Picture) and the perception that Affleck was snubbed for director. The joke requires audience awareness of the Affleck Oscar discourse. Cute but context-dependent.

jokes.text: Guess what? You wasted a lot of money on that dress. / Oh, actually, it was my grandmother's. She made it out of parachute silk while hiding from the Germans.
jokes.setup: Criss says Liz wasted money on a dress she's not using.
jokes.punchline: The dress is actually her grandmother's, made from parachute silk while hiding from the Germans — a detail that transforms what seemed like a practical argument into an emotionally devastating and historically significant object.
jokes.explanation: A perfect misdirection joke that also works as genuine character depth. The escalation of detail — grandmother's → parachute silk → hiding from the Germans — builds to an ending that's simultaneously funny and touching. Criss's 'Shut up!' is presumably the beat that follows this revelation.

jokes.text: Shut up!
jokes.setup: Liz reveals the dress is her grandmother's, made from parachute silk while hiding from Germans.
jokes.punchline: Criss's stunned 'Shut up!' — the informal expression of disbelief — is the comedic button to a piece of information that is both emotionally resonant and historically dramatic.
jokes.explanation: Works as a reaction beat but it's a standard reaction. The humor is carried by the previous joke; this is the button rather than a standalone comedic moment.

jokes.text: Liz, it's okay to be a human woman. / No, it's not! It's the worst! Because of society!
jokes.setup: Criss gives Liz permission to want a special day.
jokes.punchline: Liz agrees that being a human woman is the worst 'because of society' — an admirably vague and sweeping attribution of blame that is both feminist and self-defeating.
jokes.explanation: 'It's the worst! Because of society!' is a great Liz Lemon line — it's the right feminist sentiment expressed with maximum incoherence. 'Because of society' as a complete explanation is funny and true to how she operates. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: And why did I find this hidden under your underwear ball? / Oh, Rosenbear. He never got enough time in his garden before he passed.
jokes.setup: Liz finds something hidden — revealed to be the childhood teddy bear 'Sol Rosenbear' from the earlier cutaway.
jokes.punchline: Criss has Liz's childhood teddy bear (from Sol Rosenbear's wedding fantasy) and has developed his own relationship with it — referring to Rosenbear's 'garden' and mourning he didn't get enough time there before he 'passed.'
jokes.explanation: A brilliant callback that rewards attentive viewing. The Sol Rosenbear joke from the flashback pays off here — but the twist is that CRISS has the bear, and he's grieving Rosenbear's inability to tend his garden. The detail of 'underwear ball' as a hiding place and 'he never got enough time in his garden before he passed' are both great. This is the show's love story in miniature — Criss has been taking care of Liz's childhood bear. One of the episode's best moments.

jokes.text: I want today to be special. God, do you have any idea how hard it was to get you to admit that? 'I forgot my birth certificate. Let's invite Dennis.' Oh, you were playing me. / 'I'll wear my stupid turtleneck!'
jokes.setup: Criss reveals he was manipulating Liz into wanting a real wedding.
jokes.punchline: The 'forgotten birth certificate' and 'invited Dennis' were deliberate provocations. Liz realizes and responds with 'Wait, you think it's stupid?' about the turtleneck — still focused on the wrong thing.
jokes.explanation: Good structural payoff. Criss's manipulation plan recontextualizes all the earlier 'accidents' as deliberate. The button — Liz immediately fixating on whether he called her turtleneck stupid — is perfect Liz Lemon priority inversion.

jokes.text: We need rings and flowers, and I'm gonna put on deodorant, and you're gonna wear a suit that makes you look like a little marzipan candy man!
jokes.setup: Liz decides to do the wedding properly.
jokes.punchline: 'Marzipan candy man' — a very specific, very sweet (literally) compliment for how Criss looks in a suit.
jokes.explanation: Liz expressing love through a food-related compliment is perfect character comedy. 'Marzipan candy man' is an unusually sweet and specific comparison — it says something both about Criss's appearance and Liz's reference points (confectionery). Highly quotable.

jokes.text: 'Moses of Maryland,' page one. 'Open on: Interior Maryland slave shack, the year 18--' / Aah!
jokes.setup: Tracy has decided to read the Harriet Tubman script.
jokes.punchline: He screams in terror at the first page — either the content or the format has frightened him. The idea that he's terrified by 'Interior Maryland slave shack, year 18--' before even finishing the scene description is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A good callback to the Tubman pitch — Tracy has now read page one and is already traumatized. The sudden scream after reading the script heading is a strong physical comedy beat.

jokes.text: We aren't so different, you and I. You grew up in the Bronx. I grew up Interior Maryland slave shack, the year 18.
jokes.setup: Tracy's imagination version of Harriet Tubman is trying to connect with him.
jokes.punchline: She draws a parallel between Tracy's Bronx upbringing and 'Interior Maryland slave shack, the year 18' — the format of a screenplay's scene description being used as a real location is the meta-joke.
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly clever. 'I grew up Interior Maryland slave shack, the year 18' takes a screenplay slug line and uses it as a literal biographical fact — Harriet Tubman speaking in script format. The joke is absurdist AND meta-referential AND deeply dark. Comparing antebellum slavery to growing up in the Bronx is simultaneously the parallel and the joke. One of the episode's most clever moments.

jokes.text: And while I dreamed of becoming the first woman to surf around the world -- / Really? Is that what you think I did? / I only read the first page of the script! / Use context clues!
jokes.setup: Tracy's imagined Harriet Tubman begins to describe her dreams.
jokes.punchline: She claims to have dreamed of surfing around the world. Tracy's imagination has fabricated Harriet Tubman's goals from incomplete script reading — he literally only read one page and is filling in the rest himself.
jokes.explanation: A layered joke about Tracy's ignorance manifesting in his unconscious mind. 'I only read the first page of the script!' as an explanation for why his Harriet Tubman hallucination wants to surf around the world is genuinely funny. 'Use context clues!' from imaginary Tubman is a perfect frustrated-teacher button.

jokes.text: Why else would Harriet Tubman look and sound like your boss, Jim Dennison? / Oh, come on! You know that's wrong!
jokes.setup: The imagined Harriet Tubman explains her presence.
jokes.punchline: She points out that she looks like 'his boss, Jim Dennison' — the wrong name for his actual boss (Liz Lemon), which is both a casting meta-joke (Harriet Tubman played by someone who looks like a white executive?) and an in-world confusion.
jokes.explanation: A meta-casting joke that works on two levels — Tracy's mind can't even correctly identify his boss's name, and his hallucination is calling attention to the conceit of the sequence. 'Oh, come on! You know that's wrong!' is a good reaction.

jokes.text: Wait a minute, if this is my mind, I should be able to control you. / No, no, that only works in dreams. / Eat a corn on the cob and make it sexy!
jokes.setup: Tracy realizes this is his own mind and tries to control the hallucination.
jokes.punchline: His test of control is demanding that imaginary Harriet Tubman eat corn on the cob 'and make it sexy' — the most bizarre and specific test case imaginable.
jokes.explanation: A great joke. Of all the things Tracy could have tested his mind-control powers with, 'eat a corn on the cob and make it sexy' to Harriet Tubman is exactly the right choice. It's absurd, specific, slightly uncomfortable, and very Tracy. The corn specificity (not just 'eat something') is what makes it great. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: No, my homie -- I can say that because I'm you. / It doesn't matter if you're healthy. At any moment you could still get hit by a cab just crossing the street.
jokes.setup: Harriet Tubman tries to comfort Tracy about his good health.
jokes.punchline: She invokes cab accidents as the reassuring alternative cause of death — and justifies calling him 'homie' because she IS him.
jokes.explanation: The 'I can say that because I'm you' meta-logic is funny, and the pivot to 'get hit by a cab' as comfort is good. The joke works in the context of the hallucination sequence.

jokes.text: Right. So there's still many ways I could die. I could fall into a manhole or I could forget my chimpanzee's birthday!
jokes.setup: Imaginary Tubman points out Tracy could still die despite good health.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's list of potential deaths: manhole → forgetting his chimpanzee's birthday. The second item implies both that he owns a chimpanzee and that the chimpanzee would kill him for forgetting its birthday.
jokes.explanation: A great joke. The list starts with a mundane hazard (manhole) and escalates to 'forgetting my chimpanzee's birthday' — which packs in the information that (1) Tracy owns a chimpanzee, (2) the chimpanzee has lethal feelings about birthdays, and (3) Tracy considers this a realistic mortal risk. The implied violence of the birthday-forgetting is the kicker.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, Tracy! Are you okay? / I almost died! I've never been better. / Okay, good, 'cause I'm kind of in a rush. I'm getting married! / Liz Lemon is getting married? / Harry Truman was right! Anything's possible!
jokes.setup: Liz finds Tracy passed out. He says he almost died.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's response to almost dying is 'I've never been better.' Then upon hearing Liz is getting married, he invokes Harry Truman — implying that Liz Lemon getting married is more improbable than the famous Truman/Dewey upset election.
jokes.explanation: The Truman reference is perfectly chosen — 'anything's possible' from the Truman upset is applied to Liz's marriage as the most unlikely event Tracy can imagine. 'I've never been better' after 'I almost died' is also a clean joke. A strong two-beat moment.

jokes.text: A super-expensive period piece starring a middle-aged woman? No one's gonna want to see it! And I'm probably not gonna be alive when it comes out! Now, let's go buy a blimp and scout locations!
jokes.setup: Tracy explains why the Tubman biopic is the most irresponsible choice he can make.
jokes.punchline: He's excited by the guaranteed failure and his own expected premature death before release — then immediately pivots to buying a blimp for scouting.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's logic is inverted but perfect — he chooses the worst possible project specifically because it's the worst. 'I'm probably not gonna be alive when it comes out' is darkly funny self-awareness. 'Let's go buy a blimp' as a sudden escalation is very Tracy.

jokes.text: It's 30 minutes away. I'll be there in 10.
jokes.setup: Jack is told the City Hall wedding is 30 minutes away.
jokes.punchline: Jack matter-of-factly states he'll be there in 10 minutes — not commenting on the physics of this, simply stating it as fact. He has resources and will to bend spacetime.
jokes.explanation: A clean Jack Donaghy character joke. His calm certainty about the impossible travel time is very Jack — he has resources that make physical limitations irrelevant. Maximum economy.

jokes.text: ♪ Just in time ♪ / Navy. Gray. Maroon. Gray. Am I depressed? Later!
jokes.setup: Jack rushes to pick a suit for the wedding.
jokes.punchline: He goes through suit colors (navy, gray, maroon, gray), stops to wonder if the gray choices indicate clinical depression, then dismisses the question with 'Later!' — a beautifully compact moment of Jack's narcissistic self-analysis interrupted by action.
jokes.explanation: A compact, brilliant character moment. Jack uses the song 'Just in Time' as his rushing soundtrack, stops to briefly consider whether his color choices indicate depression, then snaps himself out of it with 'Later!' The self-diagnosis-and-dismissal is perfect Jack Donaghy — he's aware of his psychological complexity but too busy for it. 'Am I depressed? Later!' is a highly quotable button.

jokes.text: Oh, you'll do quite nicely. Come on, come on, come on, come on! Black Dennis, start the car!
jokes.setup: Jack has chosen a suit and is rushing to City Hall.
jokes.punchline: Jack has somehow gotten Dennis (or 'Black Dennis') to drive him — the callback to Dennis is funny, and 'Black Dennis, start the car!' as a command delivered in Jack's imperious way is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'Black Dennis' is a running gag payoff — and Jack yelling the name in his command voice is funny. The baby is apparently in the car as the driver, which is implied absurdity.

jokes.text: What? It's the only white dress I own. / But your hair! / I'm a princess!
jokes.setup: Liz arrives in a wedding dress.
jokes.punchline: Criss's concern about 'your hair' (implying it's disastrous) is met with Liz's triumphant 'I'm a princess!' — her hair situation presumably contrasts wildly with her self-image, but she doesn't care.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the grandmother's dress pays off here. 'I'm a princess!' delivered with complete conviction despite what sounds like chaotic hair is a great character beat. The visual of Liz in the parachute silk dress with hair apparently in disarray is the joke, and her pride in it is the punchline.

jokes.text: Tito was a drug dealer the police shot in the face. / In Riverside Park. Where we first met. / It's perfect.
jokes.setup: The officiant asks if they'll be exchanging rings. The ring is explained.
jokes.punchline: The ring apparently belonged to 'Tito, a drug dealer the police shot in the face.' This ring — from a specific violent crime scene — is in Riverside Park, where they first met. Liz declares it 'perfect.'
jokes.explanation: A beautifully dark and romantic joke simultaneously. The ring from a murdered drug dealer ('shot in the face' being the key detail), found at the site of their first meeting, is simultaneously grim and genuinely sweet. 'It's perfect' lands as both ironic and sincere. One of the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: 'But you see,' said Roark quietly, 'I've chosen the work I want to do. And I can find joy only if I do my work in the best way possible to me.'
jokes.setup: The officiant asks Liz if she takes Criss as her husband. She pauses... then reads.
jokes.punchline: Instead of 'I do,' Liz reads from Ayn Rand's 'The Fountainhead' as her vows — deeply in character and completely absurd as a wedding speech.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant character joke. Liz Lemon, incapable of expressing emotion directly, reads Ayn Rand's individualist hero Howard Roark's speech as her wedding vow. It's the most Liz Lemon possible way to say 'I love you' — mediated through literature, slightly pretentious, but also genuinely meaningful in context. The pause makes it land perfectly. Justifies 8.7.

jokes.text: "'But you see,' said Roark quietly, 'I've chosen the work I want to do. And I can find joy only if I do my work in the best way possible to me.'"
jokes.setup: It's time for Criss to say his vows.
jokes.punchline: Criss reads his 'vows' — which are actually a passage from Ayn Rand's 'The Fountainhead,' spoken by protagonist Howard Roark. Using an Ayn Rand quote as wedding vows is either deeply romantic (if sincere) or deeply funny (in context of 30 Rock's satirical universe).
jokes.explanation: The Fountainhead quote as wedding vows is a subtle literary joke — Roark's individualism applied to the context of marriage is inherently ironic. It also works as character comedy for Criss, who is clearly an earnest weirdo. The solemnity of the moment with the content being Ayn Rand is the joke.

jokes.text: Oh! My lip is caught in the grill!
jokes.setup: The wedding ceremony concludes and people begin to celebrate.
jokes.punchline: Someone's lip gets caught in something (presumably a grill or gate) during the celebration — a slapstick injury in the middle of a tender moment.
jokes.explanation: A quick physical comedy beat that punctures the romantic moment. Works as a tonal interrupter but isn't particularly inventive on the page. Gets a rewatch bonus for likely being visually funnier than it reads.

jokes.text: Lemon, earlier today, I took a hard look at where life has led me, and I didn't like what I saw. But now, looking at you, I realize -- / That anything's possible? / You know, I'm attractive. I've got cheekbones and a pair you can do something with.
jokes.setup: Jack begins a heartfelt speech about perspective, seemingly leading to a warm conclusion about Liz.
jokes.punchline: Liz feeds him the expected sentimental line ('anything's possible?'), but Jack's actual realization is purely narcissistic — he's concluded that he's physically attractive and has good cheekbones.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and one of the best Jack Donaghy jokes in the series. The setup perfectly mimics a romantic/inspirational speech — Jack's build-up, the pause, Liz's expectant 'anything's possible?', and then the reveal that Jack's epiphany was about his own cheekbones. 'I've got cheekbones and a pair you can do something with' is an exceptional line. The misdirection is perfectly structured, the character integration is flawless, and the joke is highly quotable. This is what an 8+ joke looks like.

jokes.text: I'm just saying, from a grateful nation, thank you, Liz Lemon.
jokes.setup: Jack has just concluded that he's attractive by looking at Liz on her wedding day.
jokes.punchline: He thanks Liz 'from a grateful nation' — as if her getting married was a public service that proved his own attractiveness to America.
jokes.explanation: The button to the cheekbones joke. 'From a grateful nation' as a sign-off for Jack's narcissistic gratitude is perfectly calibrated. It implies Liz's existence has served national morale by making Jack feel attractive. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: Black Dennis got some cop's gun!
jokes.setup: The wedding is concluding on a joyful note.
jokes.punchline: The final line of the episode — Dennis announces that the baby, Black Dennis, has somehow acquired a police officer's weapon.
jokes.explanation: A perfect episode-closing joke. The joyful wedding conclusion is punctuated by the information that the baby has stolen a gun from a cop. The line does enormous work in six words — it confirms everything we feared about Dennis as a father, provides a dark comedy button to the episode's sentimental climax, and rewards the audience for remembering 'Black Dennis' from the opening. 'Some cop's gun' (not 'a gun') implies multiple cops were present and one of them lost their weapon to an infant. Exceptional economy and character work.

tmdb_overview: After an encounter with Dennis Duffy, Liz and Criss decide to take drastic measures to start a family. As Liz looks toward the future, Jack and Jenna evaluate their own self-worth, and Tracy laments a shocking medical diagnosis.
insight: Season 7's densest episode: 77 jokes in 26 minutes hits late-run peak form.
